excerpt_en: Anthropic reports third-quarter stands at $16.8 billion ahead of its IPO.
content_en:
Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion as it prepares for a highly anticipated initial public offering reportedly slated for November, according to people familiar with the matter.

Revenue rose from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, with first-quarter revenue at $4.7 billion, the people said, adding that Anthropic said it was profitable on an adjusted basis in the third quarter.

The company also told investors it was cash-flow positive, generating $1.70 in revenue for every dollar spent on computing power during the third quarter, according to the Financial Times. Investors expect Anthropic to reach $110 billion in annualized revenue by year-end, according to The Wall Street Journal.

CNBC previously reported that the Claude maker planned to disclose its third-quarter financial results for the first time at a meeting with potential investors, including institutional investors, citing two people familiar with the matter.

title: Anthropic report on how AI is changing employment at the startup: decline of entry-level technical hiring, productivity boom across departments, and more
excerpt: Anthropic report on how AI is changing employment at the startup: decline of entry-level technical hiring, productivity boom across departments, and more
title_en: Anthropic report on how AI is changing employment at the startup: decline of entry-level technical hiring, productivity boom across departments, and more
excerpt_en: Anthropic report on how AI is changing employment at the startup: decline of entry-level technical hiring, productivity boom across departments, and more
content_en:
*Nathan Wilmers, Regina Catipon, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory*

How has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy.

## Key findings

- Anthropic has been hiring for a smaller share of junior technical positions. This occurred as hours worked by AI agents relative to employees rapidly expanded. By August interactive AI agent hours outnumbered employees’ 6 to 1.
- As AI agents diffused through the company, Anthropic began producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts. Following the same employee over time, output rose as they adopted new AI tools.
- This acceleration makes human attention the bottleneck for agent output. Even among non-technical employees, reading all the output of their Claude agents would take half their work week. In response, employees turn to “meta-work,” of building visibility tools and monitoring agent pipelines.
- Changes in work organization are reflected in shifting priorities among hiring managers, who increasingly emphasize autonomy and judgment, relative to technical domain expertise and implementation.

## Introduction

What transformations of work and employment can we expect under increasingly powerful AI? Anthropic is worth studying because it has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI. Agents flit through Slack chats and schedule meetings. They autonomously fix bugs and collectively tackle huge engineering projects. Agent hours worked outnumber human hours 6 to 1. Changes happening at Anthropic now give advanced signals about a possible future of work and employment.

This report draws on comprehensive internal Anthropic data covering employment, AI use, output metrics, employee surveys, internal communication patterns, employee calendar data, and hiring decision records. It contextualizes these quantitative data with 17 employee interviews.

We find that even as the company grows, relative hiring in junior technical positions has slowed. Productivity for both engineers and non-technical employees has leapt up and did so sharply when they adopted coding agents. Hiring managers increasingly emphasize applicants’ autonomy and judgement relative to specific technical expertise. A defining feature of working in an AI-heavy organization is constant pressure to streamline oneself out of this bottleneck position when possible. One engineer described work as facing “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention.” Employees at Anthropic remain critical. But the nature of their contributions has changed.

Anthropic has responded to these changes by setting up an early warning system to track jobs at risk of disruption, and as jobs evolve the company has prioritized internal redeployments. These actions, taken at the frontier of both AI development and workplace change, show how specific organizational commitments can shape the impact of AI on employment. But they also raise difficult questions about exactly what those commitments should be.

## Labor demand at the frontier

Anthropic has expanded rapidly. But it has hired less per dollar of revenue than an earlier generation of large tech companies. At five years old, Anthropic takes in between 2–4 times as much revenue per employee as Meta and Google as they crested in their own rapid growth.<sup>1</sup>

What jobs are missing? Within Anthropic, discussion of a decline in demand for junior technical employees emerged in core technical functions in January 2026. The teams that relied most heavily on Claude in their own work found that writing code and finding bugs could increasingly be offloaded to Claude. Newly capable models accelerated this perception: “the thing that raised eyebrows was the uplift for performance engineers in particular and it basically overnight changed what we were looking for.”

By April, engineering and research teams had deemphasized hiring for lower band technical positions. When surveyed in the same month, a majority of managers described hiring for a different set of skills due to AI. Around a third of ML and a fifth of SWE managers reported hiring less due to AI.

The shift in employment shares is striking. Figure 1 shows that the share of junior-level employees in technical departments at Anthropic slipped from 21% to 14% since early 2025. The proportion of junior technical hires fell even faster, from 27% to 9%. Postings for juniors have fallen particularly sharply since December 2025.

At the same time, the overall employment share of technical departments within Anthropic has fallen, from 61% to 56% in the last year. As the company expands, technical hiring has continued growing in absolute terms, but intensive hiring in sales, finance, and recruiting has outpaced it. Part of this shift is the natural expansion of business functions as the company scales. Part could reflect coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves. For example, a sales representative designed a custom dashboard and pipeline tailored to their work: “a build like this was out of my wheelhouse, especially with the UI, connecting all the tools, the MCPs. But I built this probably in three to four hours, just iterating on it.” Coding-focused AI agent sessions for non-technical employees (identified as those with no code commits at baseline, excluding new hires) leapt from 2 per month in August 2025 to 90 in May 2026.

Yet this shift in hiring composition is not only a story about automated coding allowing it to diffuse to other domain experts. Within technical departments, the share of employees not actively coding (defined as those making no code commits in the prior 30 days) fell by almost half over the year through April 2026. Part of this is due to a thinning share of non-engineers: the ratio of engineers to product managers, for example, sits at around 17 to 1 and has increased since 2025. The number of commits from managers has also doubled. The supervising and coordinating roles within technical teams increasingly involve building and shipping code.

One area in which non-technical hiring has not accelerated is in the administrative functions that typically scale with a company’s size. A combination of agent assistants, automated review and ticket service outsourcing has left Anthropic clerical-light even as it has grown rapidly. A financial manager built a purchase request review agent and explained to colleagues “it's just trying to find the things that take a lot of hours so they can focus on the other stuff.”

Even clerical work tightly connected to in-person interaction has grown slowly. An executive assistant, who built a personal assistant agent for scheduling and email triage, explained: “I think we've already moved past the point of Claude augmenting away the really entry-level admin type role,” and instead focused their work on higher-order “chief of staff” tasks.

These changes have already involved reallocation: employees working at the company for at least a year were 50% more likely to move across departments each month in 2026 than they were in 2025. Whole teams have also been reallocated as they handed off their work to agents. Consider one product design team, which wrote content like the greetings on Claude.ai: “Hello night owl;” “Coffee and Claude time?” In spring 2026, the team developed a context graph that effectively guided agents to write compelling product content. This “scaled the team out,” its manager explained, but also raised the question of what was left for human writers. The team then rotated into agent prompting and began writing model evals and prompts for Claude. “Writers who used language to drive human behavior are now using it to drive Claude behavior.”

title: Survey of Anthropic staffers and US adults: 39% of US adults vs. 91% of staffers expect AI will be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030, and more

title_en: Survey of Anthropic staffers and US adults: 39% of US adults vs. 91% of staffers expect AI will be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030, and more
excerpt_en: Survey of Anthropic staffers and US adults: 39% of US adults vs. 91% of staffers expect AI will be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030, and more
content_en:
*Szymon Sacher, Tess Cotter, Charles I. Jones, Anton Korinek, Peter McCrory*

## **Key findings**

1. US adults expect AI capabilities to advance rapidly in the coming years; Anthropic staff expect even faster progress; 39% of US adults and 91% of staff expect that AI will be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030.
2. Anthropic staff expect much larger productivity gains from AI on the tasks it is well-suited for. Among US adults who use AI at work, 26% say a task takes a quarter of the time or less with AI, compared to 59% of Anthropic staff.
3. When it comes to their own job, over half of Anthropic staff expect AI to be able to do at least 80% of their current work by 2030, compared with 5% of US workers.
4. Among both US workers and Anthropic staff, people who expect AI to do more of their own work anticipate higher unemployment. While there are differences in beliefs about future capabilities, the perceived link between how AI might change one’s own job and broader unemployment is very similar for both groups.

## **Introduction**

How will AI reshape the economy in the years ahead? AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, and the possibility that future AI models may be able to build their own successors (recursive self-improvement) could further accelerate the rate of progress. How quickly this might materialize and to what extent is unclear. Forecasts vary widely and are fiercely debated.

What is the core source of disagreement about AI's future impact on the economy? Is it principally due to differences in beliefs about how quickly AI capabilities will improve? Or does it reflect disagreement about how quickly and in what form those capabilities translate to real-world adoption? Which views on the future path of AI are consistent with rapid economic growth?

This note presents new survey evidence on these questions. In August 2026, we surveyed two groups: a sample of US adults that was nationally representative and Anthropic staff.<sup>1</sup> The questions covered, among other things, AI’s capabilities, how widely it will be used, how much time it saves, how autonomous it will be, and how difficult it will be for a displaced worker to find a job in a different occupation.<sup>2</sup> Anthropic staff build and use frontier AI every day. The second survey therefore shows how people closest to the technology anticipate its future, both in capabilities and in broader economic impact.

We report the following main findings. First, the two groups largely agree about what AI can do today but disagree about the pace of future progress. Anthropic staff expect capabilities to advance faster, AI to be used more widely and with less human involvement, and the time it saves on a task to be much larger. For example, 91% of staff expect AI to be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030, compared to 39% of US adults.

Second, there are sharp differences concerning people's own jobs. On average, staff members expect AI to be able to do 75% of their current work by 2030, compared to 28% for US workers overall.

Third, the two groups seem to reason about the labor market in a similar way: people who expect AI to do more of their own work in the future forecast higher unemployment. And, at the same level of expected AI automation of their own work, both groups forecast about the same unemployment rate.

## **What people expect AI to do**

### **Capabilities**

We first investigate expectations about AI capabilities. We asked when AI will be able to do each of eight tasks as well as a skilled professional, from writing routine emails to making a Nobel-level scientific discovery. US adults and Anthropic staff largely agree on what AI can do today, particularly when it comes to more complex tasks. Both groups rank tasks in nearly the same order of difficulty (Figure 1, panel A).

The groups disagree on the path of future AI progress. For example, around a quarter of US adults and Anthropic staff think that AI can design, conduct, and publish scientific studies today. But by next year, 9 in 10 staff expect this to be feasible for AI as compared to just 38% for the general public. By 2030, 39% of US adults expect AI to be able to make a Nobel-level discovery (panel C), compared with 91% of staff. What is perhaps the most striking difference, depending on the task, between 19 and 40% of US adults say AI will *never* be able to do a given task, compared with at most 2% of staff.

In part, differences in views reflect differences in frequency of AI use. Among those who use AI at work regularly (about a fifth of respondents), 56% expect AI to be able to do at least seven of the eight named tasks by 2030. This is substantially higher than among all US adults (41%) and among those who have never used an AI tool (28%), but still well short of the staff view (96%).

## **Adoption and its obstacles**

The impact of AI on the economy is not solely determined by raw capabilities. People and businesses need to actually use AI, which takes time and experimentation. Of the work tasks AI will be able to do, US adults expect that 42% will be done with AI by 2030. Anthropic staff expect noticeably faster diffusion over the next few years, with AI used for 65% of all tasks for which it could be used.

To understand what might hold back AI adoption at work, we asked US adults to choose up to three obstacles from a list of nine that they expect to be the biggest. The general public expects that people's preferences and rules, more than the technological constraints, may be what holds adoption back (Figure 2). “Customers preferring to deal with a person” was the obstacle selected most often, followed by “data privacy and security concerns,” “AI not being reliable enough,” and “laws, regulations or liability.”


Notably, US adults who use AI regularly at work rank data privacy and security concerns first (42% consider it among the top 3 obstacles, compared with 37% among the rest) and see customer preferences to deal with humans as slightly less important (37% vs 42%).

## **How autonomous AI will be**

The impact of AI on the labor market will in part depend on whether AI completes complex tasks autonomously or in collaboration with a human. The former tends to displace human workers. Alternatively, when AI complements human capabilities, workers become more productive. To get a sense for anticipated automation versus augmentation in 2030 among Anthropic staff and the general public, we asked how AI and humans will work together on various tasks ranging from email drafting to legal contracting by 2030. At Anthropic, the vast majority of staff say that by 2030 AI will either complete tasks alone or with a worker evaluating the work (Figure 3). By contrast, 4 in 10 US adults instead expect that humans will do most of the work themselves or with some AI help.

#### Time savings

How much AI raises output depends not only on which tasks it can do and how widely it is used, but also on how much faster and better it does them. A technology that is just good enough to replace workers—what Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019) call a "so-so" technology—displaces work without much increase in GDP. By contrast, a technology that completes tasks at a small fraction of cost or in a fraction of time can meaningfully raise GDP.

To measure perceptions about the productivity lift from AI, we asked the general public and Anthropic staff how long a task for which AI is well suited takes with AI, compared with doing it without AI. A task done in half the time corresponds to a doubling of output per hour.<sup>3</sup>

Anthropic staff report much larger expected savings, with 85% saying that it takes half the time or less. Among US adults who use AI at work, the typical answer is half the time, and 29% say the task takes just as long or longer, while only 5% of staff say so. Among US adults, 26% of those who use AI at work say a task takes a quarter of the time or less, and 21% of those who do not use AI

content_en:
Apple updated its App Review Guidelines today with a series of changes meant to strengthen protections against harmful content and deceptive app review practices. Here are the details.

## A bit of context

Over the past year alone, there has been no shortage of reports and controversies involving apps that skirt Apple’s App Review Guidelines and expose users, including minors, to harmful or inappropriate content.

In January, the Tech Transparency Project (TTP) identified dozens of AI-powered “nudify” apps on the App Store.

The group published a follow-up investigation in April, revealing that Apple’s App Store search suggestions and advertisements were also directing users to such apps. In July, San Francisco officials ordered Apple to remove eight apps capable of generating nonconsensual intimate imagery.

Also in July, a 9to5Mac investigation uncovered dozens of apps disguising gambling platforms as simple games and utilities to evade App Store review, many of which were available to children.

These apps behaved as advertised when accessed from outside Brazil, but revealed hidden betting platforms when opened from Brazilian IP addresses.

And then there was the Grok controversy, which saw Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used to generate nonconsensual sexualized images of women and minors, prompting lawmakers and advocacy groups to call on Apple to remove X and Grok from the App Store. Apple later confirmed that it had privately warned xAI that Grok could be removed unless the company addressed the issue.

Today, Apple updated its App Review Guidelines in an attempt to address problems such as these.

## Apple’s updated App Review Guidelines

Under Section 1.2, which covers user-generated content, the guidelines now read (changes in bold):

Apps **that enable users to create, generate, upload, share, or otherwise contribute** content present particular challenges, **including** intellectual property infringement, **nonconsensual intimate imagery, and** anonymous bullying.


Apple’s new terms add that “Developers who fail to implement appropriate safeguards or fail to remediate identified violations after notice may be considered in violation of the Developer Code of Conduct.”

In another particularly important change, Apple strengthened its rules against so-called ‘bait-and-switch’ apps, which “misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as “nudification” — after approval,” as the company puts it.

The newly created section 2.5.19 reads:

Don’t include any hidden, dormant, or undocumented features in your app; your app’s functionality should be clear to end users and App Review. Attempting to hide undocumented features in your app binary, such as through code obfuscation or other methods, is grounds for removal of your app from the App Store and termination of your developer account.


While the prohibition on hidden functionality was already present in Section 2.3.1, Apple has now made the rule more explicit, specifically calling out code obfuscation and emphasizing that violations can lead to an app’s removal and the termination of the developer’s account.

Finally, under Section 5 (Legal), Apple also strengthened its language around apps that facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children, explicitly stating that they “will be removed from the App Store and blocked from alternative distribution.”

To read Apple’s updated App Review Guidelines, follow this link.

# How Itaú is building generative AI for its entire customer base

With ia.i, a conversational interface, and the IARA governance platform, Itaú is applying its AI First strategy to customers and employees — in one of Brazil’s most regulated sectors.

Creating a close, personalized experience for millions of customers in a country like Brazil is, first and foremost, a question of simplicity rather than of models.

“Much of it is about making something simple, direct, and useful, delivering a direct benefit to the customer, and making the technology almost unnoticeable,” says Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO of Itaú.

The standard he describes is demanding: the solution must solve a real everyday problem and be direct, simple, and memorable. Technology serves as the means, never as the centerpiece of the experience.

There is demand for this. A study by Itaú in partnership with Grupo Consumoteca shows that 80% of Brazilians want to better organize their financial lives and seek more effective support for decisions, and that 65% would like technologies that act as a financial copilot, providing ongoing guidance.

“OpenAI’s models were very important in delivering this experience, because they were able to operate across this range of solutions.”

The journey began in 2024, when the bank introduced the first Inteligência Itaú capabilities for specific financial needs. ia.i is the next stage: a complete conversational layer, activated by text or voice, bringing interactions related to checking accounts, credit, cards, insurance, and other services into one environment — and connecting customers to specialized human support whenever needed.

This breadth was precisely what guided the choice of models.

“OpenAI’s models were very important in delivering this experience, because they were able to operate across this range of solutions,” Mazzei explains. “From the simplest ones, which need to be efficient in cost and latency, to more complex solutions, where reasoning and all the necessary grounding are required to provide an appropriate answer.”

Having a range of models — rather than a single model — made it possible to deliver the complete solution in one product. At the center of this experience is Customer DNA, a layer of financial context that helps the bank understand the needs, habits, and life stages of approximately 70 million customers. Under governance and responsible AI controls, GPT models are among the components that help maintain and enrich this representation, making interactions progressively more relevant.

The solution rests on three principles: interactivity, multimodality — text, voice, image, and clicks in the same experience — and individualization.

With approximately 300,000 customers in the first phase, the bank entered a period of learning about the real relationship between customer and product.

“We can understand how customers begin to use this product more deeply and see how it can directly benefit each person’s daily financial life,” says Mazzei. Its presence extends across the journey: from a question about an expense in an account statement to investment advice and convenient transactions on WhatsApp.

“The financial world often has products that are not so straightforward and need this context, this simpler relationship with money.”

Behind the visible experiences is an architectural decision. To operate AI at the scale of a bank, Itaú built IARA — a governance and orchestration platform that gives teams controlled access to different models in line with internal policies. OpenAI is among the model providers available in this environment.

This layer supports solutions such as the legal department’s, where the platform automates document reading, analysis, and interpretation. The solution operates on a repository of more than 90 million documents and executes more than 2 million tasks per month, with efficiency gains of 20% to 80% in stages of the department’s processes.

“It is essential that this information be preserved, remain within the bank’s context, and access models in a secure, governed way, with an understanding of token-use efficiency so that the entire solution is economically viable for the bank,” Mazzei says.

IARA addresses three problems at once: cost control per token, accuracy of responses, and application of responsible AI policies. In such a regulated sector, this makes it possible to move quickly while maintaining control.

“When we talk about Responsible AI at the bank, it is a discipline we take great care with,” he says. “We need customers to interact with the bank and our responses to align with our values and culture.” This includes reducing any risk of bias that may arise in frontier models.

Responsible AI principles guide the entire lifecycle of solutions, from development to continuous monitoring, aiming to ensure safety, transparency, ethics, and regulatory compliance as the technology scales.

“IARA is a fundamental platform, because it ensures we can have governance and observability in a highly regulated environment.”

The bank’s AI First strategy extends beyond end customers. The same intelligence layer that supports ia.i also assists specialists, managers, and customer service teams.

Mazzei describes a range extending from automating simple tasks to performing work that was previously unfeasible — but adds value to customer relationships: summaries before meetings, meeting preparation, understanding a specific issue, and developing plans and alternatives that were previously less obvious and time-consuming.

The bank has significant expectations for this implementation: three times more time available for customer relationships, service up to twice as fast, and conversations up to three times more effective.

“This set of tools in the hands of relationship managers allows us to focus on what matters most: creating value for our customers.”

- ia.i reached approximately 300,000 customers in its first phase, covering everything from convenient transactions to investment advice, activated by text or voice.
- The IARA platform makes different models available to the bank’s teams with governance, observability, cost control per token, and enforcement of Responsible AI.
- The legal solution operates on more than 90 million documents and executes more than 2 million tasks per month, with efficiency gains of 20% to 80%.
- Using a range of models made it possible to serve both cost- and latency-sensitive cases and those requiring deeper reasoning; GPT‑5.x models are part of Customer DNA, which provides financial context for approximately 70 million customers.

- Measure the experience by its simplicity, rather than sophistication. The goal is for the technology to go unnoticed and the benefit to be apparent.
- Choose a range of models, rather than a single one. Real journeys combine low-latency interactions with decisions that require reasoning.
- Build the governance layer before scaling. Observability, cost control, and responsible AI make scale viable in regulated sectors.
- Treat bias and cultural alignment as product requirements. Responses to customers must reflect the institution’s values.
- Apply the strategy internally, too. Giving time back to teams frees up human relationships where they matter most.

- Start with concrete everyday problems, such as a question about an account statement or a simple transaction.
- Launch to an initial customer group and use it to learn actual behavior before expanding.
- Centralize model access on one platform to maintain control over costs and quality.
- Monitor token efficiency from day one — economic viability is part of the design.
- Combine conversation and navigation: not every action is best handled through natural language.

content_en:
# Teaching students to think and learn through questions

On Teachers’ Day, we celebrate those who help us learn. A good question can change the course of a lesson. It can bring an unspoken question to light, open up another way to solve a problem, or help someone recognize what they already know. Teachers do this work every day: they know their students, choose how to introduce an idea, and guide them from their first attempt to understanding.

Set in a university classroom, the campaign takes a humorous look at the changing relationship between teachers and students and celebrates the role of educators in a world with AI.

Today, we are launching the <u>**AI for Educators**</u>(opens in a new window) course in Brazilian Portuguese on OpenAI Academy, OpenAI’s free learning platform. Designed for educators in primary, secondary, and higher education, the course shows how to use AI to plan lessons, create activities and assessments, and prepare communications while preserving educators’ pedagogical judgment.

<u>Study Mode helps you explore a subject</u>(opens in a new window) step by step, with questions, hints, explanations, and checks for understanding. Developed in collaboration with teachers, scientists, and experts in pedagogy, the feature aims to encourage active participation and reflection on one’s own reasoning.

To turn on **Study Mode**, select Study from the tools menu in ChatGPT.

A student reviewing biology, for example, might ask: “I’m studying enzymes. Ask me one question at a time, wait for my answer, and help me identify what I need to review.”

Teachers can also try Study Mode with subjects they know well, looking at whether the questions encourage reasoning and whether the explanations are appropriate for their class.

In a science lesson on evaporation, for example, a teacher might ask students to investigate why clothes dry on a clothesline. After exploring the topic with Study Mode, each student writes their own explanation and a question to discuss in class, without referring back to the conversation. The teacher can use these responses to identify what needs to be revisited with the class.

This Teachers’ Day, we invite you to experiment: explore the AI for Educators course, try Study Mode, and discover how these tools can be useful in different teaching contexts. Technology can open up new ways to learn, but it is teachers who know their students, ask the most important questions, and help turn curiosity into knowledge.

### Microsoft reveals cutting-edge MAI-Base-2 model with 2T parameters

Microsoft Corp. has developed a new large language model that it says is significantly more efficient than leading open-source alternatives.

The company’s artificial intelligence research group detailed the algorithm on Thursday.

MAI-Base-2 is not a full-fledged LLM but rather a base model, a kind of no-frills prototype. Developers turn base models into LLMs by putting them through several additional rounds of training. That extra training usually focuses on adding reasoning features and safety guardrails.

The most capable open-source base model on the market today is DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base. Microsoft says that MAI-Base-2 outperformed it on a series of internal benchmarks that contained science, programming and math questions. Furthermore, MAI-Base-2 is up to 12 times more hardware-efficient by certain measures.

MAI-Base-2 features a mixture of experts, or MoE, architecture, which means that it only uses a subset of its artificial neurons to process prompts. That’s more efficient than activating the entire neural network. MAI-Base-2 has 2 trillion parameters and activates 80 billion of them when it receives a prompt.

A language model’s artificial neurons are organized into clusters called layers. Microsoft’s previous-generation base model mixed MoE layers with modules based on a less efficient design called FFN. MAI-Base-2 is made up entirely of MoE layers, which is one of the contributors to its performance.

Microsoft trained the model for 38 days using 16,000 of Nvidia Corp.’s GB200 chips. The training dataset used in the project comprised 50 trillion tokens. About a fifth of the tokens were used to train a computer vision module integrated into MAI-Base-2. The module makes the model better than its predecessor at tasks such as understanding scientific charts.

Developers train LLMs by observing the manner in which they complete tasks and providing feedback on how they can improve. That feedback, which is generated algorithmically, takes the form of a mathematical object called a gradient. The gradient travels through the layers of the model being trained and re-calibrates each one to boost its output quality.

Gradients change every time they pass through an LLM layer. Under certain circumstances, those changes cause bugs that can disrupt the training workflow. Microsoft employed a method called gradient clipping to prevent that issue from affecting MAI-Base-2. It also used Muon, a popular open-source AI tool, to speed up the training workflow.

Microsoft will license MAI-Base-2’s weights to “trusted partners” through its Azure cloud platform. Additionally, it will use the model to power a new series of LLMs. The company plans to share more information about those models in the near future.

title: AWS, Anthropic race to deploy army of specialized engineers key to proving AI spending will pay off
excerpt: AWS, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google are racing to build forward deployed engineering teams as companies seek returns on their AI investments.
title_en: AWS, Anthropic race to deploy army of specialized engineers key to proving AI spending will pay off
excerpt_en: AWS, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google are racing to build forward deployed engineering teams as companies seek returns on their AI investments.
content_en:
After spending billions building artificial intelligence, Big Tech is now spending heavily to build the human workforce needed to prove the investments are paying off.

Companies are scrambling to find specialized AI engineers who can put the technology to work inside businesses. These specialists — called forward deployed engineers, or FDEs — combine advanced AI and software expertise with an understanding of how corporations operate. They could be the key humans in the loop required to turn powerful large language models into enterprise systems that can deliver measurable business results.

Market concerns that the economics of the AI boom are not sustainable have intensified this week with many top AI-themed and memory-themed stocks from Dell to CoreWeave, AMD and Micron suffering significant short-term losses.

Amazon Web Services has committed $1 billion to a forward-deployed engineering initiative. OpenAI has launched a deployment business backed by more than $4 billion in initial investment. Anthropic is putting $100 million into a program to train 10,000 forward-deployed engineers by the end of 2027. And Accenture and Google Cloud are building a 1,000-person forward-deployed engineering workforce.

"The Street is starting to become impatient with these billions of companies who are spending on AI without getting any business outcomes," said Jeff Christian, founder of executive search firm Christian & Timbers.

Working directly with customers, FDEs navigate existing technology systems, security requirements, and organizational obstacles to turn promising AI experiments into applications companies can actually use.

At Caylent, an AWS consulting partner that embeds FDEs with customers, CEO Val Henderson said the role requires more than technical expertise.

"The hardest thing to teach is the customer EQ, without question," she said, adding that engineers also need to understand customers and businesses, navigate organizational dynamics, and exercise judgment when projects encounter unexpected problems.

### **A surge in job postings, salaries with scarce talent available**

Experienced talent is scarce, and developing that expertise can't happen overnight in a labor market race that recent hiring numbers suggest is accelerating.

U.S. job postings for FDEs surged from fewer than 200 in 2023 to approximately 1,200 in 2025 and more than 7,300 in the first nine months of 2026, according to data from labor market analytics firm Lightcast.

Median advertised salaries reached $195,456 during that period, up 40% from 2023 and more than three times the median advertised salary across all U.S. job postings.

The competition extends well beyond the companies developing AI models. Consulting firms are among the biggest recruiters, reflecting demand for engineers who can help corporate clients implement the technology.

Lightcast counted 872 unique FDE job postings from Deloitte and 688 from Accenture during the first nine months of 2026, followed by Google with 499 and KPMG with 447. The figures represent advertised positions, not completed hires.

"Demand for forward deployed engineers is rising fast, and growing wages suggest employers are competing for a limited pool of talent," said Elena Magrini, head of global research at Lightcast.

But the data also points to a potential solution.

"FDE is not an entirely new role. It shares roughly half of its skills with software engineering, creating an opportunity to tap into a much broader talent pool," said Magrini.

Technology companies and their corporate clients are investing in multiple ways to develop deployment expertise.

AWS is building its own FDE organization, drawing on experienced engineers within Amazon and AWS while also recruiting externally. The company is starting with hundreds of engineers, according to Asa Kalavade, vice president of forward-deployed engineering at AWS.

"We are investing $1 billion now because customers need this hands-on help turning their AI investments into results at speed," Kalavade said.

OpenAI is pursuing a broader enterprise deployment strategy, backed by the $4 billion in initial investment and an agreement earlier this year to acquire Tomoro, an applied AI consulting and engineering firm expected to bring approximately 150 experienced FDEs and deployment specialists into the operation.

### AI skills gap is a 'market problem'

Anthropic is taking a different approach, training engineers already employed by its customers and partners. Through its Claude Frontier Academy, the company aims to train 10,000 FDEs by the end of 2027. Its first residency cohorts include engineers from Accenture, Bain, Capgemini, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Deloitte, McKinsey, Morgan Stanley, and Novo Nordisk.

"The AI skills gap affects every customer and every partner, so it is a market problem, and Anthropic is committed to helping close it," said Steve Corfield, Anthropic's global head of business development and partnerships.

Accenture and Google Cloud, meanwhile, are building a 1,000-person FDE workforce, relying partly on retraining experienced software engineers for customer-facing AI deployment work.

"The reality is that experienced FDEs cannot simply be recruited at the scale clients need," said Ram Ramalingam, Accenture's FDE and software and platform engineering lead. Depending on their backgrounds, the company's FDE training and onboarding can take 30 to 90 days, Ramalingam said. He added that participants already have substantial software engineering experience; the program is designed to add specialized deployment capabilities rather than train beginners.

AWS also sees an opportunity to develop expertise inside customer organizations. Kalavade said many businesses already employ capable engineers but need help learning how to move AI projects into production. AWS's FDEs work alongside those teams so customers can eventually maintain and expand the systems themselves.

The challenge goes beyond technical expertise, said Corfield. "A skill in short supply is an engineer who can understand how the business works and also build the system that changes it," he said.

Anthropic believes some of that expertise can be developed through structured engineering. Its Frontier Deployed Engineer Residency borrows from medical education, pairing experienced engineers with practitioners and evaluating them on realistic enterprise deployments.

"We modeled the residency on how medicine trains doctors," Corfield said. Participants learn from practicing engineers, work on realistic cases, and are assessed before they practice on their own companies, according to Anthropic. They then receive 12 weeks of mentorship from Anthropic engineers while working on Claude projects. The first full credentials are expected in early 2027.

### Too soon to analyze results from deployments

According to Christian, experienced FDEs can help expand the workforce by leading teams of less-experienced engineers. For instance, he said, those who have completed 10 to 15 successful deployments may have the judgment to supervise teams of five or six, passing along expertise gained from working through complicated customer projects.

Christian sees that mentorship model as a way to expand deployment teams without requiring an elite engineer in every position.

But Henderson said the customer-facing judgment required for complex AI deployments is particularly difficult to teach. While technical skills can be developed through training, engineers also need experience navigating real-world customer challenges.

"There is no compression algorithm for experience," Henderson said.

For Christian, the challenge comes back to the pressure from investors to produce business results. He argued that companies need engineers who can work directly with customers to translate increasingly powerful AI systems into practical applications. "The only way you can get AI to work is by human-to-human interaction," he said.

title: Amazon launches new Bee 'personal AI' devices that listen to conversations
excerpt: The $75 Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of Amazon's wearable bracelet, while the $100 Bee Eclipse attaches to a user's smartphone.
title_en: Amazon launches new Bee 'personal AI' devices that listen to conversations
excerpt_en: The $75 Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of Amazon's wearable bracelet, while the $100 Bee Eclipse attaches to a user's smartphone.
content_en:
Amazon on Thursday unveiled two new Bee listening devices, including a wearable and a credit card-sized voice recorder, marking its latest push into the AI gadget market.

The Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of Amazon's existing wearable that can either be worn on a wrist or clipped to clothing. Similar to earlier generations, the Bee Frontier has up to seven days of battery life, but it's also more expensive, costing $75 compared with its $50 predecessor.

Amazon acquired Bee, a San Francisco startup known for its always-listening bracelet, in July 2025 for an undisclosed amount. Bee bracelets are equipped with artificial intelligence and microphones that can record, transcribe and analyze conversations.

The dual mics on the Bee Frontier have upgraded noise filtering, "so it can take note of what matters and ignore what doesn't, even in noisy environments like a crowded restaurant or open office," Amazon said in a blog post.

Amazon also debuted the $100 Bee Eclipse, which functions like other Bee devices, but instead of being worn, the credit card-sized gadget magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone.

The Bee Frontier is available Thursday, while the Bee Eclipse "will be available soon," the company said.

Amazon is refreshing its Bee lineup as tech companies gear up for the holiday season with a slew of new AI hardware. Amazon nixed its budget-friendly Fire family of tablets in favor of three new AI-infused Alexa Tablets, while Microsoft showcased an Nvidia-powered Windows laptop and Apple unveiled its HomeView smart home hub with Siri AI.

The Bee gadgets will compete with other AI wearables already on the market.

Meta has seen growing momentum from its smart glasses that are infused with AI and have a built-in camera. The glasses have also generated widespread privacy and civil rights concerns from users, advocacy groups and lawmakers.

Meta has also announced a palm-sized pendant called Muse Charm that runs its latest Muse AI assistant. Plaud developed a card-shaped note-taking device, and Friend offers an AI necklace.

Amazon's voice-activated Echo smart speaker got users comfortable with interacting with its Alexa AI assistant, but the devices were designed to only start listening when prompted with a so-called wake word.

When turned on, Bee devices are always recording. Amazon says this enables key features like conversation summaries and the ability to "review memories from the past few days to remember what you discussed." It can also track "trends or themes that recur" to give personalized goals or actions.

With a Bee Pro subscription, which costs $12 per month, users can get unlimited conversation summaries and daily memories as well as integrations with Amazon's webstore, its Alexa+ AI assistant and third-party apps. For example, if a user mentions they need to buy dish soap, they might see the product recommended on the Amazon homepage, or in the Bee mobile and desktop apps.

The company said Bee devices are designed so that "no one, including Amazon, can access your data." Users can delete their transcripts and summaries at any time and "no audio is ever stored," Amazon said.

An LED light signals when Bee gadgets are recording, Amazon said.

title_en: Amazon’s Bee launches two new personal AI devices, starting at $75
excerpt_en: Amazon-owned Bee has launched its first new AI devices since its acquisition, including an updated wearable and a credit-card-sized recorder that attaches to smartphones. The devices can summarize conversations, create to-do lists, and integrate with Alexa and Amazon shopping, with prices starting at $74.99.
content_en:
Amazon’s personal AI wearable maker, Bee, is announcing its first new products since being acquired by the retail giant last year. The tech company on Thursday introduced the Bee Frontier, the next generation of its device that can be worn on the wrist or pinned to clothes, along with Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of your smartphone.

The latter puts Bee into more direct competition with AI devices like the Plaud Note or Pocket, but at a lower price point — the Bee Frontier is $74.99, compared with $159 for the Plaud Note (or $189 for the Note Pro), or $129 for the Pocket AI device.

The Bee Frontier will come in Onyx, Lavender, and Sage, while the $99.99 Bee Eclipse will be offered in Silver, Midnight, Honey, and Blush.

Like the original Bee, the idea with the new devices is to leverage AI to take notes from your everyday conversations, allowing you to remember the important things that were said, and then turn those into actionable to-dos, summaries, and insights.

For instance, if you discussed making plans with friends, the Bee would remember the date and time you agreed on, then create a calendar invite. You could also use the Bee to take lecture notes in class, or to jot down the care plan you discussed with a doctor, among other things.

All Bee devices can create conversation summaries and recaps for free, and offer 14 days of memory. With an $11.99 per month Bee Pro subscription, users receive unlimited conversation summaries and integrations with Amazon.com, Alexa+, and third-party applications. Pro users also get suggested to-dos, daily memories, a personal chat assistant, and conversation templates.

To make all this possible, Bee devices use a private computing security architecture, which doesn’t store the raw audio from your conversations. Instead, audio is processed in real time and then deleted. Transcripts of the conversation are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls, which means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you manually and intentionally share them.

In addition, you can opt to connect the Bee to Alexa, allowing your Echo device to use its ability to identify your voice, a feature called Voice ID, to recognize when you’re speaking. It can then record your conversations to provide Bee’s insights. (This aspect of Bee is optional, and Amazon notes you can delete transcripts and summaries at any time.)

With its new connections to Amazon.com and Alexa, Bee users can make purchases from Amazon or ask Alexa for their Bee insights, summaries, or to-dos hands-free.

Bee also works with your existing productivity software, like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, so it can draft emails, set up meetings, surface action items, and more.

Plus, you can upload photos to Bee or connect it with Apple’s HealthKit to add a picture of your overall wellness to be integrated into your provided insights.

The Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse both have just one button that turns the device off and on, and include an indicator light when it’s summarizing a conversation. The Frontier also offers IP67 water resistance, up to seven days of battery life, USB-C charging, and dual microphones with advanced noise filtering.

All Bee devices come with a companion mobile app, which has also been newly redesigned, plus a new desktop app.

The Bee Frontier is available now on Amazon, and the Eclipse will be available soon thereafter.

content_en:
European AI funding in H1 2026 was dominated by the UK, France and Germany, with large investments driving the overall total, while smaller rounds supported emerging startups and the growing adoption of AI across industries.

European AI funding in H1 2026 was characterised by a high
concentration of capital in a few large transactions, alongside a
broad base of smaller investments. Several rounds exceeded €500 million,
highlighting the capital-intensive nature of advanced AI research and
infrastructure development. At the same time, numerous seed and pre-seed rounds
reflected continued investment in early-stage AI companies.

Geographically, the UK led in both funding value and deal activity, followed by France and Germany. Together, these three markets attracted the vast majority of capital, while smaller investments across the Netherlands, Spain, Switzerland, the Nordics and Central and Eastern Europe reflected the broader geographical spread of Europe's AI ecosystem.

The industry also showed increasing diversification, with
funding supporting AI models, computing hardware and data infrastructure,
alongside applications in healthcare, manufacturing, financial services and
cybersecurity.

For further insights into funding trends across the European
technology ecosystem, check out Tech.eu's Funding Explorer, free and open to
everyone.

1

Ineffable Intelligence (UK)

Amount raised in H1 2026: $1.1B

Ineffable Intelligence is a UK-based AI research company working to develop systems capable of learning autonomously.

Its approach centres on reinforcement learning, aiming to create a “superlearner” that can continuously acquire new knowledge and skills through experience rather than relying on human-generated data. The company is exploring an alternative path towards advanced artificial intelligence, with a focus on systems that can discover knowledge independently.

In H1 2026, Ineffable Intelligence raised $1.1 billion to support the development of its autonomous learning technology and advance its research into superintelligence.

2

Advanced Machine Intelligence (France)

Amount raised in H1 2026: $1B

Paris-based Advanced Machine Intelligence (AMI Labs) is developing AI systems designed to understand and predict how the physical world works.

The company focuses on world models as an alternative to traditional large language models. Rather than relying primarily on text-based predictions, its technology aims to enable machines to reason about real-world environments, anticipate outcomes and develop a deeper understanding of physical reality.

AMI Labs secured $1 billion in H1 2026 to advance its world model research and build teams across Paris, New York, Montreal and Singapore.

3

Mistral AI (France)

Amount raised in H1 2026: $830M

Mistral AI is a French artificial intelligence company developing large language models and generative AI solutions for businesses, developers and public institutions.

Positioned as a European alternative to major US AI providers, the company focuses on open-weight models, customisable AI systems and infrastructure that gives organisations greater control over their data and technology. Its strategy includes expanding European computing capacity to support AI model training and deployment while reducing reliance on external cloud providers.

During H1 2026, Mistral AI secured $830 million in debt financing to purchase 13,800 Nvidia GPUs for its first data centre in France, supporting the expansion of its AI infrastructure.

4

Recursive Superintelligence (UK)

Amount raised in H1 2026: $650M

Recursive Superintelligence is a London-based AI startup developing systems capable of improving their own intelligence without continuous human intervention.

The company is exploring recursive self-improvement as a path towards advanced artificial intelligence. Its initial focus is on developing AI that can improve other AI systems through automated research, with longer-term ambitions to apply these methods across scientific disciplines.

In H1 2026, Recursive Superintelligence raised $650 million to advance its research into self-improving AI systems and develop technology for automated scientific discovery.

5

ElevenLabs (UK)

Amount raised in H1 2026: $561M

London-headquartered ElevenLabs was founded in 2022 and specialises in AI-generated voice and audio technology.

Its platform enables users to generate realistic speech, clone voices, dub content into multiple languages and create sound effects. Originally focused on text-to-speech technology, the company has expanded into conversational AI, offering voice agents for customer support, sales, marketing and internal business operations. Its technology is used by businesses, developers and content creators worldwide.

ElevenLabs raised approximately $561 million across funding transactions in H1 2026 to expand its enterprise AI agents, advance research into conversational models and audio technology, and support international growth.

6

Parloa (Germany)

Amount raised in H1 2026: $350M

Berlin-based Parloa develops conversational AI technology that enables businesses to automate customer interactions across voice, chat and messaging channels.

The company provides an AI agent management platform that combines speech recognition and natural language understanding to handle customer enquiries and support tasks. Its technology is used by companies including Allianz, Booking.com and SAP, helping customer service teams manage interactions at scale while reducing reliance on traditional call centre processes.

In H1 2026, Parloa raised $350 million in a Series D round to accelerate its international expansion, particularly in the US and Europe, and strengthen its presence in key markets.

7

PhysicsX (UK)

PhysicsX is a London-based technology company applying artificial intelligence to engineering and industrial design.

The company develops AI-native software that enables engineers to simulate complex physical systems, test design alternatives and optimise products more efficiently. By reducing simulation processes that traditionally take weeks or months to seconds, PhysicsX aims to address engineering bottlenecks in industries including aerospace, manufacturing, semiconductors and defence. Its technology supports faster product development and more efficient hardware innovation.

PhysicsX secured $300 million in H1 2026 to further develop its platform, advance AI research, expand its US operations and establish an office in Singapore.

Its approach focuses on overcoming memory bandwidth constraints and improving the economics of running complex AI workloads, combining chip architecture, AI research and semiconductor engineering to support more demanding applications.

title: British Business Bank invests £180M across AI and deeptech funds

title_en: British Business Bank invests £180M across AI and deeptech funds
excerpt_en: The British Business Bank has today announced it is investing £180m across six AI and deeptech VC funds, as investors continue to pile into the two hot sectors.The state-owned investor is investing £3...
content_en:
The British Business Bank has today announced it is investing £180m across six AI and deeptech VC funds, as investors continue to pile into the two hot sectors.

The state-owned investor is investing £35m in London-based Crane Ventures Partners’ Crane III fund, which backs founders from inception to seed; it is also investing £20m in London-based Connect Ventures’ Connect V fund, which backs founders at pre-seed stages; and it’s investing £22m in Matt Clifford’s Entrepreneurs First’s early-stage fund.

It is also investing £55m in Intrepid Growth Partners’ Fund I, a specialist growth fund dedicated to AI; £26m in global investor Headline’s EU VIII fund; and £22m in Matt Miller’s Evantic Fund I.

The new investments follow the British Business Bank's announcement yesterday that is was investing £10m in Salience Labs.

The British Business Bank, which was given increased spending power last year following a government review, has also directly invested in Wayve, Kraken Techologies and PolyAI.

Leandros Kalisperas, chief investment officer, the British Business Bank, said: “The UK has no shortage of ideas or talent. The problem is that our funding landscape does not currently match our technical excellence. This is what the Bank is changing.

"These commitments are part of our strategy to create deeper pools of funding at all stages of growth, helping companies to access greater capital domestically and allowing the UK to capture more of the economic value of its innovations.”

title_en: Vilnius-based Holo raises €5M to bring AI-powered marketing to small businesses
excerpt_en: AI marketing platform Holo has raised €5 million in a seed fundinground to further develop its marketing automation technology and reach moresmall businesses. The round was led by Market One Capital, ...
content_en:
AI marketing platform Holo has raised €5 million in a seed funding round to further develop its marketing automation technology and reach more small businesses. The round was led by Market One Capital, with participation from Silicon Gardens, FirstPick, Leonis Capital, NGL, Tekton Ventures and business angels.

Founded by Deividas Kovger and Aleksandras Urbanavicius, Holo aims to make AI-powered marketing tools more accessible to small businesses, allowing them to manage their marketing without dedicated teams. The founding team also includes Karolis Vaiginis, who leads design, and CTO Arnas Puidokas.

Holo combines marketing planning with content creation and campaign management in a single platform. To get started, business owners enter their website, allowing the system to analyse their products or services, brand identity and communication style. Based on this information and the business's goals, Holo generates a marketing plan outlining which channels to use, what campaigns to launch and which activities to prioritise.

The platform then creates marketing materials, including advertisements, social media posts, emails and SEO content, tailored to the business's brand. These are organised in a content calendar, where users can review, edit and approve materials before publication across connected channels. Businesses can also automate selected tasks, allowing campaigns to run without requiring approval at every stage.

Holo also monitors campaign performance and uses the results to recommend adjustments to future marketing activities. For example, it can suggest allocating more budget to better-performing advertisements or creating additional content in formats that generate greater reach.

The platform combines third-party AI models with its own technology, including a system that retains each business's brand identity and communication style, a strategy engine for marketing planning and a creative system informed by performance data from millions of pieces of content generated through the platform.

Holo reached $5 million in annual recurring revenue within 252 days, having raised less than €1 million before this round. The platform now serves more than 20,000 paying businesses across over 100 countries.

The new funding will be used to further develop Holo's marketing autopilot capabilities, reach more small businesses and expand its team in Vilnius.

excerpt_en: AI-powered personalfinance startup Matters has emerged from stealth with $5 million in pre-seedfunding to develop a consumer banking platform focused on helping users managetheir spending and increase...
content_en:
AI-powered personal finance startup Matters has emerged from stealth with $5 million in pre-seed funding to develop a consumer banking platform focused on helping users manage their spending and increase their savings.

The round was led by Swedish angel investor Jakob Johansson, with participation from Knut Frängsmyr (former COO of Klarna), Douglas Stark (Voi co-founder), Johan Bladh (CEO of Röko), Patrik Tran (CEO of Validio), and Per Widerstrom (CEO of Evoke).

Matters was founded by Per Österström with the aim of building an AI-native consumer bank that combines automation and personalised financial guidance to help customers improve their financial wellbeing.

The company's planned offering combines neobank services with an AI Advisor designed to help users make more informed spending decisions, increase savings and work towards their financial goals. Customers will pay a flat monthly subscription fee, while revenue streams typically retained by banks, such as interchange revenue and foreign exchange fees, will be returned to users through an accumulated cashback system.

Through this model, Matters aims to align its business interests with those of its customers, focusing on customer experience, retention and long-term loyalty.

According to Österström, traditional banking models do not always encourage better financial decisions, while Matters intends to take a different approach by making financial wellbeing more accessible.

Our goal is to build a bank that actively makes financial wellbeing available to anyone, not just those who already enjoy it,


he said, adding that the company expects to launch its first consumer product in the coming weeks.

Alongside the funding announcement, Matters has appointed Lars-Åke Norling as Chair. Norling previously served as CEO of investment and savings platform Nordnet and brings experience in regulated consumer finance and technology as Matters prepares to expand into banking.

The company is entering a market where financial management remains a challenge for many younger consumers. According to figures cited by Matters, half of Gen Z and millennials do not know where their money goes, while 80 per cent of young adults report experiencing regular financial stress. Matters aims to address these challenges through AI-powered financial guidance and automated tools.

The new funding will support the company's plans to apply for licences, expand across the EU, grow its existing team and attract users. Matters is also considering potential strategic acquisitions as part of its development plans.

Startup Reflection AI Inc. today made the weights of Beam, its first large language model, available on Hugging Face.

The company also released technical resources that will enable developers to customize the algorithm.

Originally introduced last week, Beam is one of the industry’s most advanced open-source LLMs. It features about 500 billion parameters, yet approaches the performance of models four times its size on some benchmarks. It also uses significantly less computing power and memory.

Reflection AI trained Beam over two months using several thousand high-end graphics cards. Such large-scale training runs are prone to errors that can decrease model quality. According to Reflection AI, its engineers addressed the challenge by developing a set of custom reliability optimization algorithms.

The company’s error mitigation efforts placed particular emphasis on avoiding training-inference mismatches. Those are bugs that emerge when there are slight inconsistencies in the configuration of an AI training environment’s components.

Reflection also developed a system that can automatically fix certain data quality errors. When such bugs emerge, the system reverts the training run to an earlier stage and continues from there instead of starting over from scratch. The company says that its optimizations enabled it to train Beam with practically zero cluster downtime.

Beam’s newly released weights are available in multiple versions. There’s a standard edition and several scaled-down variants that keep information in smaller units of data. That arrangement, which is known as quantization, trades off some output quality for increased hardware efficiency.

The weights are available alongside training recipes, code templates that enable users to fine-tune the model. A vibe coding startup, for example, could create a fine-tuning workflow that enhances the model’s programming capabilities. The recipes are joined by tools that can be used to measure how customizations change Beam’s capabilities and safety guardrails.

Reflection AI has also released a drafter model for Beam. It can be used to implement speculative decoding, an inference approach designed to lower hardware usage. The basic idea behind the method is to use a lightweight LLM, the drafter model, to generate the initial version of a prompt response. Beam checks the output for errors before displaying it to the user.

Performing inference in a hardware-efficient manner requires developers to use a software tool called a serving engine. Adapting an LLM to a given serving engine can involve a significant amount of work.

Today’s release includes ready-to-use Beam configurations for several popular serving engines. Developers also have access to fused kernels, code snippets that compress multiple inference calculations into a single operation to speed up processing.

Reflection AI plans to follow up the launch by releasing additional training recipes in the coming days. They will enable Beam to refine its own output quality using an approach known as self-distillation. Additionally, the company intends to share some of the lessons it gleaned while developing the model in the form of contributions to open-source AI tools.

content_en:
### ServiceNow adds AI agent controls and employee automation tools

ServiceNow Inc. today announced new controls for governing artificial intelligence agents alongside updates to its EmployeeWorks information portal (pictured) that let employees build specialized assistants and automate routine tasks without writing code.

The announcements address two connected challenges for businesses expanding their use of autonomous AI: giving workers tools that can act across enterprise systems and ensuring those tools stay within approved boundaries.

The centerpiece of the governance announcement is AI Passport, a cryptographically signed credential that defines an agent’s identity, permitted actions, accessible systems and accountable owner. Issued through ServiceNow’s AI Control Tower governance platform, it is designed to carry those permissions across agents, tools and vendors, with checks performed as work executes.

“Without that baseline, every guardrail is just advisory,” said Nenshad Bardoliwalla, senior vice president of AI products at ServiceNow.

The company says identifying agents and monitoring their behavior aren’t enough without enforceable limits on their authority. AI Passport draws on business context from ServiceNow’s configuration management database, governance policies and workflow approvals to establish those limits.

In a demonstration, ServiceNow configured a third-party customer service agent to process refunds below $25 while disabling unrelated capabilities. An $18 refund proceeded automatically, but a $40 request was rejected at runtime because it exceeded the threshold for human review.

### ‘Dimmer switch’ for agents

The approach supports graduated responses when agents exceed their authority. Organizations can pause an agent by revoking session tokens, restrict its access to approved tools and endpoints or deactivate it by revoking credentials. Agents can subsequently be restored with a recorded explanation.

“It’s more like a dimmer switch,” Bardoliwalla said. “You monitor, you pause, you restrict, and eventually, if necessary, you deactivate.”

Nvidia Corp. is a design and launch partner, linking AI Passport with its Open Agent Safety Platform, including the OpenShell secure runtime and Sentry security framework. The integration connects enterprise policies with enforcement within the infrastructure where agents operate.

The central implementation challenge is “making your enterprise policy meaningful at the point of execution,” said Itay Ozery, Nvidia’s director of product marketing for cybersecurity.

ServiceNow said AI Passport uses open specifications so other governance products, identity providers and enforcement systems can issue and verify credentials. It is intended to support third-party agents as well as ServiceNow’s own.

AI Control Tower is also expanding discovery, observability and financial oversight. Additions include shadow AI detection, more than 400 vendor connectors for discovery, access mapping and monitoring of agent behavior. Cost capabilities track spending by user, department and runtime, while connecting consumption and quality with business value.

AI Cost Management consolidates spending on frontier models, AI embedded in software services, hyperscalers and data center graphics processing units. A separate Operational Resilience offering brings governance, risk and security together for financial institutions.

### Employee controls

The EmployeeWorks updates extend that governance strategy into everyday work. Its third-generation employee-focused AI harness combines reasoning, memory and connections to business systems, with administrator-defined controls over what employees can build and access.

Productivity Assistants target work requiring context specific to a job or business function. Employees can customize behavior, information sources and tools. Initial offerings include research and calendaring assistants, along with human resources-focused assistants for talent insights, HR business partners and managers.

Productivity Routines handle repeatable work in the background. A sales employee, for example, could automate reviewing upcoming meetings, researching prospects and assembling account materials before the workday begins.

“There’s no coding required. It’s drag and configure and deploy all within these guardrails,” said Bhavin Shah, senior vice president of ServiceNow’s employee experience group.

For developers, the new ToolSmith environment builds tools and integrations from natural-language instructions. ServiceNow said ToolSmith is trained on more than 75,000 application programming interfaces and can plan integrations, retrieve logs, suggest fixes and support testing. Shah said it uses governed connectors to read and write enterprise data in a preproduction development environment.

A Conversations API lets organizations embed EmployeeWorks capabilities in internal applications, kiosks, messaging services and other AI applications.

NTT Data Inc. is using AI Control Tower to address shadow IT and is beginning to adopt EmployeeWorks, said Jamie Robins, head of the company’s ServiceNow practice. Among the challenges the company faces are overlapping AI tools, duplicate use cases and fragmented employee systems. NTT Data hopes to simplify employees’ access to services while consolidation continues. “It takes time to consolidate processes, systems, tools, data,” he said during a product briefing.

Pricing combines seat-based licenses with bundled AI credits called assists. Customers needing additional capacity can purchase more credits, and EmployeeWorks uses the same currency as ServiceNow’s other AI products. Bardoliwalla said the model aims to balance predictable budgets with flexibility for customers whose usage grows beyond their initial entitlement.

AI Passport, shadow AI detection and AI Cost Management will be available later this quarter. Operational Resilience for financial services is available now. The new EmployeeWorks assistants, routines, harness, ToolSmith and Conversations API are in controlled availability.
