title_en: Tech Race Summit participants warn of obstacles to turning AI pilots into profits [Sponsored]
excerpt_en: Early in his talk, Georgios Chatzimilioudis, a Solutions Engineer at Oracle, asked the audience to raise a hand if they expected their business to use more AI in three years than today. Hands went up....
content_en:
Early in his talk, Georgios Chatzimilioudis, a Solutions Engineer at Oracle, asked the audience to raise a hand if they expected their business to use more AI in three years than today. Hands went up. He asked who expected to use more than one model, and the hands stayed up. Then he asked who was confident they knew which model, chip, platform or framework would matter most to their business in three years. Every hand came down.

This set the tone for the inaugural Tech Race Summit, organised by SOFTSWISS, which brought together over 1,500 participants from fintechs, e-commerce companies, iGaming operators and other digital players facing the same pressures in high-load industries.

## Organisational gap in AI adoption

Businesses worldwide face significant uncertainty, given the breakneck speed of technological innovation. Beyond just keeping up with the newest AI-based tech, they are also facing challenging organisational and strategic decisions about how and where to implement AI to ensure the biggest positive impact on the bottom line.

Buying access to a model is straightforward, but giving it reliable company data, deciding what it can do and proving its work justifies the expense is harder.

Sergey Khurson, Principal Solutions Architect at AWS, said 88 per cent of organisations use AI in at least one part of their business, but only 8 per cent have reached advanced maturity, where AI runs in production across the business rather than in isolated pilots.

The 2027 iGaming Trends Report, based on input from more than 500 industry professionals and 65 experts, points to the same gap, with  AI moving deeper into engineering, fraud prevention, customer support, compliance and infrastructure. The challenge is shifting from whether companies can deploy AI to whether they can integrate it reliably, govern it and demonstrate measurable business value.

One solution discussed was to define work specifically around AI tools with strict boundaries that guard against project creep and protect value for money.

## Pilots without a business case 


There is also another curious issue facing businesses, mainly that AI experiments can survive long after their purpose has become unclear. Viktor Vedmich, Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, described “zombie projects” that continue indefinitely, consuming resources without a decision on whether to expand or stop them.

Vedmich argued for shared platforms between teams and fewer projects, chosen by potential value and the effort required. Before work begins, a company should define what success means and when management will decide on a wider rollout.

Putting programmes under the CEO or COO, with targets tied to revenue and margins, makes those decisions harder to evade. It also forces the business to confront whether it is automating work that is worth doing in the first place.

## Managing data in the AI age 


Another problem is that a capable model has limited value if it cannot find or interpret the information it needs. Oracle’s Chatzimilioudis cited a Gartner report, suggesting that 63 per cent of organisations lack the data management practices AI requires. His remedy was to give data clear owners, record its origins and set rules for access. For companies holding sensitive financial or customer data, he argued for bringing AI to the data, rather than repeatedly copying information into new stores.

Cloudflare put that approach into practice, starting with finding out what employees needed, according to Field CTO Michael Tremante. The company set up an email address where staff could ask an agent team for help. This helped create a shared context layer, built around a GitHub repository, which supplied knowledge and reused across tasks. 

The result was a central source of information and data, which drove adoption and laid the foundation for more complex tools.

## Ensuring usability for all 


The next step was giving staff more powerful tools, so Cloudflare preconfigured the open-source tool OpenCode with enterprise model accounts, which helped engineers. However, non-technical employees struggled with setup and authentication, so the company then built Cloudflare OS, an internal tool intended to be usable from an employee’s first day.

Tremante said that rolling out Cloudflare OS meant that a new marketing hire, for example, could write a blog post in the company’s voice on day one, because the tool already held all corporate guidelines, key facts and approval process.

## Cost of access and responsibility

Beyond the usability puzzle, the cost is the big elephant in the room. Choosing the right model for each task is key when costs are hard to predict.

Cloudfare’s Tremante questioned the logic of sending every request to the most powerful, and expensive, option when simpler models can often do the job. To address this, the company routes requests between models and runs open-source alternatives on its own infrastructure to keep costs down.

At the Tech Race Summit, the CTO panel was divided over whether productivity gains justified current spending. Some warned that modest improvements would eventually be difficult to finance; while others saw the cost as small compared to what their best engineers could now produce.

In addition to the cost issue, understanding who is held accountable when AI takes on more workstreams, was another theme that loomed large at the conference. The issue of responsibility is especially key, given that the reliability and veracity of AI output remains difficult to verify.

Andrey Doronichev, the former Google executive now running AI-native pharma company Bioptic, shared one approach to improve quality of AI-based output. At Bioptic, human pharma experts maintain a bank of questions and answers used to test agents and improve their performance, effectively defining what a good result looks like as the system is built.

This is one way of addressing the quality issue to enable AI to produce more reliable results. However, the industry consensus is that ultimate responsibility for the work performed by AI will remain with the business.

Tech Race Summit delegates agreed that for now, there needs to be a human in the loop, ensuring that an output is good enough to deliver, and understanding the process of how it was achieved, and how much it cost well enough to make that call.

content_en:
European AI infrastructure company Nebius says it has struck deals with a number of early-stage UK AI labs as it looks to accelerate its compute and infrastructure offering in the UK.

Nebius, which is sometimes referred to as a neocloud, builds and operates data centres, packing them with GPUs, then offers access to these data centres to AI and enterprise companies needing compute power, as well as offering them specialised software to run AI applications.

Earlier this year, Nebius announced a £1.7bn UK build-out across new sites, along wtth an expansion of its London hub, which is its major European R&D and go-to-market hub.

Nebius, which is headquartered in Amsterdam and has bagged multi-billion-dollar contracts with Meta and Microsoft to supply them with AI infrastructure, has four data centre sites in the UK. Nebius, which has also struck compute deals with Revolut and Prima Mente, also has its own data centres in Finland and France.

Nebius general manager, EMEA, Gary Tierney, said Nebius wanted to “continue to look to expand” in the UK, referencing its talent density. He said: “We are working with some really exciting AI labs that are coming out of the UK.”

Tierney did not provide specific details on which UK AI labs it was working with but said they were in stealth or just came out of stealth.

London-based AI lab Ineffable Intelligence, founded by former DeepMind bigwig David Silver; Inherent, founded by former DeepMind, Microsoft and White House staff; and Recursive Superintelligence, co-founded by high-profile German computer scientist Richard Socher, are examples of UK AI startups coming out of stealth this year.

Ineffable Intelligence has struck a deal with Google Cloud to be its preferred cloud partner.

Asked more broadly about the public backlash against data centres in the UK, Tierney said: “I don’t think that is ever a reason for us not to invest in a region” pointing to its investment in the UK.

Separately, Tierney said he was pleased the UK government was planning to ease restrictive non-compete clauses in workers' employment contracts.

He added: “It’s not necessarily been a problem for us. But we service the startup market. And when you look at that non-compete not existing in the US, you see the startup market is moving way quicker.

“Here, now with so much great talent appearing and being able to raise funds but they can’t attract talent in London, because of this non-compete, if that goes away, I think you are going to see an emergence of a lot more labs, a lot more frontier builders here in the UK."

title: TSMC posts record profit for a sixth straight quarter, beating estimates on AI boom
excerpt: TSMC reported its third-quarter earnings on Thursday.
title_en: TSMC posts record profit for a sixth straight quarter, beating estimates on AI boom
excerpt_en: TSMC reported its third-quarter earnings on Thursday.
content_en:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. on Thursday reported a record third-quarter profit that beat estimates, powered by an unrelenting global appetite for AI chips.

Here are TSMC's third-quarter results against LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate:

- Revenue: 1.49 trillion new Taiwan dollars ($46.36 billion) vs. NT$1.47 trillion
- Net Income: NT$763.1 billion vs. NT$746.34 billion expected

The world's largest contract chipmaker posted a record net profit for a sixth straight quarter, reporting 68.7% surge in the reported quarter from a year earlier.

TSMC's third-quarter operating margin came in at 58.7%, exceeding the upper end of its guidance range of 58%, showcasing the pricing power enjoyed by the company as the AI boom fuels demand for semiconductors.

TSMC forecast fourth-quarter revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, representing a 14% sequential increase and a 58% jump from a year earlier at the midpoint of its guidance range, according to the company's earnings call.

The chipmaker expects its capital expenditure from 2026 to 2028 to be significantly higher than in the previous three years, as it continues to ramp up investments to support growing customer demand.

TSMC's stronger-than-expected results and upgraded full-year revenue outlook underscore how demand for advanced chips continues to outpace its production capacity, with the company's elevated capital spending reflecting confidence in sustained growth over the coming years, Sravan Kundojjala, an analyst at SemiAnalysis, told CNBC via email.

TSMC expects its fourth-quarter business to be supported by continued strong demand for its advanced chipmaking technologies, including the ramp-up of its 2-nanometer process.

Kundojjala also highlighted TSMC's careful approach to capacity expansion, adding that the chipmaker is assessing whether customers have the financing and supporting components needed to deploy AI systems.

"Even after those checks, TSMC says demand remains well above its supply capacity," he said, adding that it reinforces confidence in the AI buildout while ensuring investment decisions reflect customers' ability to deploy the chips they order.

Advanced technologies, defined as 7-nanometer and more advanced technologies, made up for 79% of TSMC's total wafer revenue in the reported. The 3-nanometer chips accounted for the largest share of its revenue in the third quarter at 33%, followed by 5- and 7-nanometer chips.

By platform, high-performance computing accounted for the largest share of revenue at 68%, followed by smartphones at 21%. Meanwhile, automotive was the fastest-growing segment on a quarter-on-quarter basis, with 23% growth rate.

TSMC said demand for AI chips remains strong, driven by the growing adoption of agentic AI and open-source AI models, which are expected to make AI more accessible and fuel demand for advanced semiconductors.

The company's free cash flow surged to NT$476.56 billion in the third quarter, from NT$139.38 billion a year ago.

TSMC also pointed to rising demand for AI accelerators, processors used in agentic AI applications and networking, adding that semiconductors are set to play an increasingly important role in the global AI supply chain.

TSMC also said it had completed construction of its second fab in Arizona and is installing equipment, with mass production expected to begin in the third quarter of 2027, slightly ahead of its previous schedule.

TSMC board approved NT$7.00 cash dividend for the second quarter. During its second-quarter earnings announcement in July, TSMC had outlined plans to expand its U.S. manufacturing footprint, including a total planned investment of $265 billion in Arizona.

The chipmaker is also reportedly considering expanding beyond Arizona, evaluating a potential investment in Texas as it looks to further strengthen its U.S. manufacturing presence.

content_en:
### Mistlabs takes its Ambi AI system out of beta on Apple devices with $26M in funding

Ambient intelligence startup Mistlabs Ltd. today brought its Ambi artificial intelligence system out of beta test on Apple Inc. devices, backed by $26 million in new funding.

Ambi is designed to act without being asked. Chief Executive Peter Mo said most AI platforms are built to complete tasks, and Mistlabs wants to see what becomes possible once software can “understand, reason and act in real time.” Ambi’s actions can sometimes come “before the user even thinks to ask,” he said.

To do that, Ambi learns about a person from the conversations it hears on their iPhone, Apple Watch or Mac, and Mistlabs said the software’s read on how that person likes to work sharpens over time. None of it is locked to a single device. Whatever Ambi is in the middle of follows the user from the Mac to the phone or watch.

A user who sets up a Routine hands a recurring job to several agents at once, and those agents work from everything Ambi has picked up about that person. In one example the company gives, someone sits through a meeting about competitors while the agents fact-check what is being said as the discussion unfolds. Ambi may have compared the rival products and drafted a proposal on the user’s MacBook before anyone leaves the room. The agents keep at it once the meeting ends, flagging missing information or new developments as the project moves along.

Further out, Mistlabs wants Ambi agents to negotiate with each other. The capability is due in the coming months and would come into play when two people using the software sit in the same meeting. Each agent would draw on what it knows about its own user, and together they would work out where the two sides’ priorities overlap.

Likely sticking points would surface as well. From there the agents are meant to bargain toward a result both people can accept, all while the conversation is still going. Users set the permissions that govern what their agent can do.

The $26 million raised ahead of the launch will pay for a standalone wearable Mistlabs is building to give Ambi more context about its users and their surroundings. Mo said hardware will let the system extend to “entirely new device types” over time. Luminous Ventures and Huaqin Technology Co. Ltd. led the San Francisco company’s Pre-A round. Huaqin, based in Shanghai, designs and manufactures smart devices for other brands.

Ambi is available now on Macs and on Apple devices that support iOS 18, with audio storage switched off by default. Anyone interested in the wearable can join a waitlist, and Mistlabs said the device will follow later this year.

excerpt_en: Reach Security, which develops AI-powered exposure management tools for securing enterprise systems, raised a $50M+ Series B led by Top Tier Capital Partners
content_en:
**Reach Security has secured more than $50m in a Series B round led by Top Tier Capital Partners, while unveiling Reach Everywhere, a launch that pushes its security control intelligence into every environment where defensive decisions are made.**

Alongside lead investor Top Tier Capital Partners, the round drew backing from Ballistic Ventures, In-Q-Tel, M12, Microsoft’s Venture Fund and existing investors. Reach plans to direct the capital towards product development, broader integration partnerships, expansion overseas and further growth across US enterprise and federal markets.

The raise follows a year in which the firm’s customer count doubled, with Autodesk, Insurity, MPS and Ensemble Health Partners among the businesses using its technology.

The investment lands as attackers gain ground. VulnCheck’s State of Exploitation 1H-2026 report showed that under 1.3% of vulnerabilities are actually exploited in the wild, meaning the real challenge lies in reaction time rather than discovery.

CrowdStrike’s 2026 Global Threat Report recorded an 89% jump in AI-enabled adversary activity, with breakout times falling to as little as 27 seconds, and AI is now linking exploits into previously unseen attack paths.

Reach responds by helping operations teams concentrate only on exposures and misconfigurations that remain genuinely reachable, ignoring those already neutralised by existing tools. Its AI independently reviews and adjusts each control, allowing defences to absorb growing attack volumes without extra staff.

When an adversary, or an AI agent a customer has deployed against its own estate, finds a way in, Reach shuts that route by reconfiguring security products the organisation already owns.

Reach Everywhere carries these insights into exposure management programmes, security operations centres, incident response processes, compliance platforms and frontier AI security environments, using the Reach API, its MCP server and a widening network of technology partners. Teams can therefore reprioritise backlogs and adjust controls inside the tools they already use.

A key early use case supports exposure management teams struggling with vulnerabilities that cannot be patched at the pace AI uncovers them. Reach locates, verifies and continuously tracks compensating controls, confirming they are active, up to date, enforcing policy and positioned in the correct attack path.

Where a change is safe, it routes the fix through ServiceNow, Jira or its own staged automation, testing it in a controlled environment first. An independent ROI study by TAG Infosphere found customers saved over 160 hours each week across control review, posture assessment and incident investigation, alongside a 156% return.

Reach describes itself as the trusted source of truth for enterprise security controls. Its deterministic AI continuously finds, analyses, validates and optimises controls, helping organisations map attack paths, cut risk and demonstrate that protections perform as expected. Through its API and AI-powered MCP server, AI systems can draw on live, validated control health data in place of stale inventories, exports or assumptions.

Reach Security CEO and co-founder Garrett Hamilton said, “What is old is new again in security. AI has given attackers better economics and a lower barrier to entry, but it has also given defenders a chance to use their home field advantage more than ever. Defending at enterprise scale requires an accurate understanding of what your defenses are actually doing. You can’t afford to get that wrong.

“That’s why a source of truth for your security controls matters so much: which ones are reducing exposure, which ones are falling short, and which ones can do more. That clarity is valuable to customers and to our joint integration partners.”

Reach Security co-founder and CTO Colt Blackmore added, “A compensating control that cannot be verified is not a mitigation. It’s an assumption. At human scale, incorrect assumptions create inefficiency. At machine scale, they create risk.

“Whether decisions are made by analysts, automation platforms or AI agents, the underlying truth about security control health must remain consistent, accurate and continuously validated. Our vision is to provide a trusted source of truth for security controls that makes those systems reliable, effective and safe to operate.”

excerpt_en: London-based Scarlet, which certifies AI and software for medical devices, raised a $50M Series B led by Headline to support its US and Asia-Pacific expansion
content_en:
Scarlet, the certification body for AI and software medical devices, today announced a $50 million Series B led by Headline, with participation from new investor Notion Capital and existing investors Atomico, Creandum, Kindred Capital, and Entrepreneurs First. Nancy Xiao Mclaughlin, Partner at Headline, joins Scarlet’s board.

AI medical devices are being developed faster than certification bodies can review them. A company can train an AI diagnostic model in weeks and then wait 12 to 18 months for an assessment by experts, with another six to eight months of unnecessary delay for approval of a minor update, slowing down healthcare innovation.

Scarlet is a government-designated certification body. Among the roughly 52 such organisations designated under the EU Medical Device Regulation, it is, according to the company, the only one that specialises in software and AI, and was truly built to enable AI’s iterative development. Scarlet holds designations from the EU, the UK’s MHRA, and the US FDA, where it is recognised as a Third Party Review Organisation.

James Dewar and Jamie Cox founded Scarlet in London in 2021 after building AI medical devices at Babylon Health. The company spent its first three years working with regulators to obtain designation before issuing any certificates.

Customers upload technical documentation to Scarlet’s AI-enabled platform in any format. Qualified reviewers then assess the submission against relevant regulations and ultimately issue a certification decision, deciding whether the product can be released into the market or not.

Customers are typically building devices that use cutting-edge AI such as LLMs and computer-vision models, and include consumer giants like Flo Health, who boast over 500 million downloads, US radiology behemoth DeepHealth, the UK’s NHS England, cancer-detection AI company Skin Analytics, and AI Scribes such as Heidi Health and Tandem, who both recently announced nine-figure Series B fundraises.

Scarlet also certifies the way AI products are actually built. Customers pay a subscription that covers ongoing surveillance, annual audits, and product changes. Because every assessment is consistent and every finding is evidenced, regulators can see the reasoning behind any certification decision at any time.

“Scarlet has built a Notified Body for the AI world. The ability to release more rapid and frequent upgrades to our medical device ensures that our patients always have access to world-class care. We want to release upgrades to our medical device twice a month. We can with Scarlet,” said Finn Stevenson, co-founder and CEO of Flok Health.

“For every day that safe and effective medical technology is not available, someone’s life takes a different course. Scarlet exists to solve this problem,” said James Dewar, Scarlet’s Co-founder & CEO.

“We’re building AI-native certification to help our customers bring cutting-edge innovation to patients around the world.”


“Scarlet helps regulation work with and for, not against, innovation. James and Jamie experienced the legacy certification process firsthand and decided to become the AI-native market enabler, starting with certifying AI and software as medical devices,” said Nancy Xiao McLaughlin, Partner at Headline.

“Scarlet has superpowers that seem at odds: they are fast, consistent, thorough, and rigorous. 

The team is devoted to its customers and takes seriously its mission to get life-saving technology to people faster. We’re excited to lead the Series B and for everything ahead.”


The funding will support Scarlet’s expansion in the United States and Asia-Pacific, growing its roster of expert AI reviewers and engineers, and expanding its certification offerings.
